title: Worms (1521)
hookLine: before the emperor, Luther refuses to recant unless shown wrong by scripture and reason

lines: A HALL OF PRINCES AND BISHOPS.
A PILE OF BOOKS ON A TABLE.
ARE THESE YOURS? WILL YOU RECANT?
cards: A hall packed with princes, bishops and knights. At the front, on a raised seat, the Holy Roman Emperor, Charles. On a table in the middle, a pile of books.
A monk in a plain habit is brought in and stood before them. An official points at the books and asks two questions. Are these yours?
And will you take back what's in them? He says yes to the first. To the second, he asks for time, and he's given one night.
The city is Worms, and the meeting is an imperial assembly.

teach.b: The next day Luther came back and gave his answer, first in German, then again in Latin. Some of his books, he said, were about plain Christian faith, and even his opponents agreed with them; how could he take those back?
Others attacked abuses. Others attacked people, and he admitted he'd sometimes been harsher than a monk should be. But recant?
Unless he was convinced by the testimony of scripture or by clear reason, he said, he could not and would not.

teach.h: CAPTIVE TO THE WORD OF GOD.
teach.b: His conscience was captive to the word of God, and to go against conscience was neither safe nor right. Early printed accounts add the line people remember: here I stand, I can do no other.

Whether he said those exact words, historians aren't sure. The idea isn't new. When the apostles were ordered to stop preaching, Peter answered, in the King James Bible: "We ought to obey God rather than men."
The next day, the emperor answered with his own statement of conscience. He would hold to the faith of his forebears, he said, and stake his kingdoms, his friends and his life on it.
Two men, each sure of his conscience, each staking his life. Luther was declared an outlaw. Christians today read Worms in different ways.
Protestants often see a man standing for scripture against power. Catholics may see a monk breaking with the church's teaching authority, and an emperor keeping faith.
What both can recognize is a person refusing to say what he didn't believe, with the whole room watching.

how: Lutherans and other Protestants remember Worms as a stand for conscience and scripture; Catholic and Lutheran churches today discuss this history together in their official dialogues.

games.why: he would not recant unless convinced by scripture or clear reason, because his conscience was captive to the word of God.

practice: Bring to mind one thing you won't say or do, even when it would be easier, something you hold to quietly.
Then picture someone who sees it differently, remember that the emperor spoke of his conscience too, and allow that they may be standing by theirs; hold both, firm and kind.
If you pray, ask for courage and gentleness together, in your own words or a line you already know.
